title: A pricing page for an architecture studio
metaTitle: What an architecture studio pricing page shows
excerpt: Show what an architecture fee includes, what it leaves out, and how to start a project. Careful clients use that page to judge fit, not to finish the arithmetic.
alt: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table, a working meeting for deciding which parts of a fee belong in public.
caption: A table where the shape of the work gets said out loud. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should an architecture practice publish a fee?
faqs.answer: Publish the shape, even when you will not publish a final number for an unseen site. Say whether you work to a percentage of the build, a fixed fee by stage, or time for early advice. Say what that money covers and what the client still has to hire. A page that only says fees are available on request forces the question you will answer on the first call anyway.

faqs.question: What should a fee page leave out?
faqs.answer: Leave out a precise quote for a site you have not seen. Leave out consultant fees you do not control, council charges, and the cost of the build, unless you are clear that those sit outside your agreement. A range can help a client judge fit. A fake exact figure creates a dispute before the survey is done.

faqs.question: Where should the pricing page send people?
faqs.answer: Send them into a project conversation with a short list of what to bring: the address, whether they own it, the use, and a rough sense of budget if they have one. The page has done its work when a mismatched client opts out and a matched client knows the next step.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An architecture studio pricing page is how a client who is judging taste before competence checks fit. They are not opening a spreadsheet. They want the shape of the fee: what is included, what is not, and how to start a project conversation.

Show that shape if they will ask for it on the first call anyway. A line that says only "fees on application" sends a careful client toward the office that will speak plainly. Taste got them to your work. The fee page tells them whether a conversation is even sensible.

## Fit comes before arithmetic

The buyer at this stage has usually seen your buildings. They are asking a coarser question than a quantity surveyor. Can we afford this kind of practice, and do they take work like ours? A percentage, a band, or a stage list answers that. A locked quote for a house they have not described yet does not.

Say the model in the first screen. "We work to a fixed fee by stage for houses and alterations." Or "Early advice is charged by time until the site and the brief are clear." Or "The design fee is a percentage of the construction cost, agreed once the brief is stable." Pick the sentence that is true. If you use more than one model, say which kind of project gets which model. A house alteration and a multi-year civic building should not share a single vague line.

Nielsen Norman Group's note on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is useful here in a practical way. Visitors read only a fraction of the words on a page. The shape of the fee has to be visible without a long read. A heading, a short stage list, and a plain sentence on exclusions will do more than an essay about the value of design.

[Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether someone can leave having learned enough to take their next step. On this page the next step is a project conversation, or a polite no. If they still have to email you to learn whether consultants are included, the page has not finished its job.

## The shape, in client language

Use stage names a client can repeat to their partner. Early advice. The design. Drawings a builder can price. Visits while the building goes up. Internal phase codes are for your office manual. The website can carry the plain list.

A workable public structure:

- How you charge: percentage, fixed stages, or time.
- What each stage produces: a feasibility note, a planning set, a builder's set, site visits.
- What a typical house or alteration requires before you will name a number.
- What sits outside the fee.
- How to start a project conversation, and what to send first.

That is the whole page. You can add a short note on how long a stage usually takes in calendar time, if you are willing to stand behind it. Keep it as a range tied to a type of project. "A single-house planning set often takes a season, not a fortnight" is a shape. A promise of six weeks for every job is how you start a dispute.

If your region uses a professional fee guide, you can say that you work with reference to it, and then explain the part a client actually feels: what they receive, and what they still pay others. Do not paste a table they cannot interpret. Do not invent a discount to look approachable.

Write the numbers you are willing to repeat. If a band for alterations in your city is something you already say on calls, it can live on the page. If the band changes with every site, say that the number comes after a look at the address, and still show the model. Hiding the model because the number moves is the mistake. The model is the fit check.

## What the fee includes

Be concrete about the work inside the agreement. Meetings to settle the brief. The drawings for the stage they are buying. The planning submission, if that is part of the offer. A set number of revisions, stated as a number, not as "unlimited collaboration." Coordination emails with the builder during the stage you have included.

Name who they will deal with. If the director leads the early design and a project architect runs the drawing set, say so. A client judging taste has already decided they like the buildings. They are now deciding whether the people who made those buildings will be on their job. The fee page is allowed to say that. It should not turn into a biography. One sentence is enough, with a link to the people page.

Say what "fixed" means if you use the word. Fixed for a defined brief, with a written change if the brief grows, is honest. Fixed no matter what happens to the site is a promise most houses will break. Clients can accept a change rule. They struggle with a surprise.

Include the ordinary extras you always provide and then forget to mention. A model, a physical material board, a planning meeting attendance. If those are in the fee, the page should say so, because competitors who charge them separately will look cheaper until the second invoice.

## What the fee does not include

The exclusions are the part that protects both sides. List them where they can be scanned, not in a footnote in pale type.

Typical lines, written only where they are true for you:

- Structural engineering, energy assessment, and other specialist consultants.
- Land survey, measured survey, and geotechnical investigation.
- Council and certification charges.
- The cost of construction, fixtures, and styling.
- Interior pieces, furniture, and garden design, unless that is actually your scope.
- Work after a stage ends, if the client pauses and returns a year later.

A client who wanted a full team under one invoice needs to see that boundary before they fall in love with a scheme. A client who already has an engineer is relieved. Either reaction is a successful page.

Do not hide a large exclusion inside a friendly sentence. "We coordinate the consultants" can mean you manage them while the client pays them, or that their fees sit inside yours. Those are different products. Use the plainer sentence.

If you sometimes include an interior scope and sometimes do not, split the line by project type. One muddy paragraph is how a pricing page recreates the phone call it was meant to shorten.

## A range judges fit. It is not a quote.

The limit of this page is simple. It cannot price an unseen site. Sloping ground, a heritage overlay, a party wall, a flood level, and a client who changes the brief will all move the fee. Say that in one sentence near the numbers, so the band is read as a fit check.

Offer the path from band to real number. "Send the address and a short note on use. We will tell you whether we are the right office, and what the first stage would cost." That is a project conversation. It is not a form that asks for their life story.

Refuse the two false versions of transparency. The first is a single number with no scope, which looks brave and becomes a fight. The second is a manifesto about value with no model at all, which looks thoughtful and tells them nothing. The useful page sits between them: a model, a boundary, and an invitation to confirm the figure on their actual site.

Keep the visual quiet. This is not the page for a fullscreen render. The work that earned their taste is already elsewhere. Here, type, a short list, and a calm table if you truly have two or three project types. Motion that reveals the number on scroll is a way to look evasive. The figure, or the clear statement that the figure comes after the address, should be on screen without a trick.

## From the fee to the conversation

Put one action on the page. "Start a project" should match the label you use in the header. Ask for the address, whether they own the property, the use, and a budget sense if they have one. Four fields, or a short email. Ten fields belong to a different problem. You are qualifying a conversation, not onboarding a contractor.

Tell them what happens next, in your own timing. "We reply within two working days to say whether we can take it, and to propose a first meeting or a first-stage fee." Use a window you will keep. Do not borrow a speed from another studio's marketing. A true slower reply is better than a fast promise you miss.

Say what the first meeting is for. To test fit. To look at the site if that is your habit. Not to produce a sketch. Clients who expect a free scheme will be disappointed in a way that poisons the job. The page can prevent that with one sentence.

If you want a reference for how plain a public page can be about a real constraint, look through [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful projects are the ones where a limit is visible beside the pictures. A fee page is the same discipline in sentences: the limit is the scope, and the picture is the list of what the money buys. Hanabi designs and builds sites in that spirit. The pricing page should be as editable as a caption, so you can correct a stage name without a rebuild.

## The offers, named one by one

A fee shape still floats if the reader cannot see which kinds of work it applies to. Houses, alterations, and interiors can share a model and still need their own boundaries. A feasibility study before a purchase is a different product from a full commission. The next page is where those offers get an outcome, a limit, and a next step, in the words the client already uses.

Read [the services page an architecture studio actually needs](/blog/the-services-page-an-architecture-studio-actually-needs) before you add a second pricing table. If the offers are still a grid of vague capabilities, another fee table will only price the fog.
